title: Lucian Freud Spent Months Finishing a Face. He Left This Tree Half Done.
standfirst: Freud wiped his brush clean after every stroke of flesh so the colour never repeated by accident. On this bare winter acacia, painted in 1975, he stopped before the bottom left corner was filled in. Nobody was waiting on him. He just walked away.

sections.heading: He Cleaned His Brush After Every Stroke. He Left This Corner Bare.
sections.body:
Freud's method on the portraits that made his name was close to a ritual. He cleaned his brush after each stroke when painting flesh, so that the colour on the canvas stayed, as it's put on his own Wikipedia page, constantly variable — no accidental repeats, no shortcuts. A sitting could run for months; some sitters came back for a year or more.

Against that discipline, Acacia is a strange object. It is a bare, sparse view of the tree in winter, and by the account of at least one specialist blogger who has catalogued his plant work in detail, the bottom left corner of the canvas was never filled in. There was no sitter to keep waiting, no gallery deadline forcing his hand. A tree does not object to being kept mid-sitting. He stopped on it anyway.

sections.heading: A Year After His First Retrospective, He Wasn't Looking at People
sections.body:
In January 1974 the Hayward Gallery gave Freud his first retrospective, at fifty, after nearly three decades of being one of Britain's most respected but least publicly exhibited painters. It showed more than 120 works spanning his career back to 1937, drew over 90,000 visitors, and then toured to Bristol, Birmingham and Leeds. The critic Michael Shepherd wrote in the Sunday Telegraph that the quality of the show was such that he simply wanted to say there were 142 works there and every one deserved looking at.

Acacia followed the next year. Freud gave his own account of why he painted plants at all: "The subject matter has always been dictated by the way my life has gone. I noticed that when I was under particular strain, I didn't feel so like staring at people or bodies all day." It's a clean explanation, and it's in his own words — but nothing in the record ties a specific strain to 1975 itself. If anything, this was the year his reputation was widening, not narrowing.

sections.heading: Plants Were the Model That Never Cancelled
sections.body:
Freud painted botanical subjects across nearly his entire working life, from a gorse sprig shown in his first solo exhibition in the 1940s to a garden scene finished in the late 1990s. A tree or a pot plant could not fail to show up, could not get bored halfway through a pose, and — unlike the sitters he worked from for months — some of them decayed fast enough to force him to work at speed instead of his usual crawl.

He was drawn to that decay rather than avoiding it. Of cyclamens he said: "They die in such a dramatic way. It's as if they fill and run over. They crash down, their stems turn to jelly and their veins harden." That is a painter describing a subject that does the work of dying for him, in full view, on his own timetable — which makes Acacia's blank corner odder still. A tree in winter isn't rushing anywhere.

sections.heading: The One Plant Collection Vienna Never Stopped Growing
sections.body:
Not all of Freud's plants were neutral subjects either. Still Life with Zimmerlinde, painted around 1950 and sold at auction in 2018 for £908,750, shows descendants of houseplants his grandfather Sigmund Freud had grown in Vienna before carrying them to London in 1938 as he fled Nazi-annexed Austria. The plants outlived the escape and kept being propagated for decades; Lucian was painting a lineage, not a prop.

It's a reminder that when this family painted a plant, the plant sometimes had its own passport. Acacia carries no such backstory that the record shows — no named garden, no inherited pot, nothing to explain why this particular tree got chosen and then abandoned partway through.

sections.heading: Two Years Later, He Went the Opposite Way for Three Years Straight
sections.body:
Whatever let him leave Acacia unfinished didn't last. Two Plants, begun in 1977 and not finished until 1980, is by most accounts of his botanical work the most laboured thing he ever painted from vegetation: a liquorice plant and a cast-iron plant rendered leaf by leaf over three years. Freud himself described how unforgiving the composition was: "When I took one tiny leaf, and changed it, it affected all other areas of it, and so on."

Set the two paintings side by side and the gap is the whole story. Within the same decade, on the same general subject, he produced the most obsessively resolved plant painting of his career and, two years earlier, one he simply put down. Nothing about the genre made that decision for him.

sections.heading: A Label Built for Fidelity, Sold on a Painting That Quit
sections.body:
The record files Acacia under Contemporary Realism, a label built on the idea of unflinching, exhaustive observation — Freud's own reputation, more or less, in two words. It sits oddly on a canvas with a corner nobody ever went back to finish. Realism, in his case, was supposed to mean the artist stayed until the subject had nothing left to hide; here he left before that happened, on a subject with nothing to hide in the first place.

That didn't stop the market. Acacia sold at auction on 22 June 2005 for 47% above its mid-estimate, according to the auction database MutualArt, which does not disclose the hammer price without registration. Someone paid a real premium for a Freud that the artist himself had abandoned — which suggests the buyers were pricing the name and the winter light, not the finish.
